content: Then all Israel gathered themselves to David to Hebron, saying, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh. {{v:2}} In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. The LORD your God said to you, ‘You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.’” {{v:3}} So all the elders of Israel came to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD. They anointed David king over Israel, according to the LORD’s word by Samuel.

facets.evidence: Connecting the tribes' phrase 'bone and your flesh' to Genesis 2:23 and then further to Christ's incarnate solidarity with humanity requires two successive typological steps not made in the passage itself.
facets.text: When all Israel comes to David saying "we are your bone and your flesh," the tribes acknowledge a kinship that binds king and people into a single body. This echoes Adam's cry over Eve ("bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh," Genesis 2:23) and points toward the deeper solidarity of Christ, the Son of David, who took our flesh so that we might become members of his body. The king is not a foreign ruler imposed from without but one of the people, sharing their nature.
facets.question: Why do the tribes call David their own bone and flesh?

facets.evidence: Evident arc of the narrative: the people cite David's prior shepherding action under Saul ('it was you who led out and brought in Israel') as the basis for now formalizing his kingship, making service-before-title the plain sense of their appeal.
facets.text: The people recall that even under Saul it was David "who led out and brought in Israel," recognizing that true kingship is proven in shepherding action long before it is formally conferred. Legitimate authority in Israel is grounded not merely in title but in faithful service already given to the community. David's anointing ratifies what his life had already demonstrated.
facets.question: What made David a true leader even before he was crowned king?

facets.evidence: While the passage explicitly calls David 'shepherd,' the leap to Jesus as the Good Shepherd fulfilling this office (John 10:11) and the theological claim that earthly rule is stewardship rather than ownership require an argument beyond what the text states.
facets.text: The LORD's own word designates David to "shepherd my people Israel," framing kingship as a pastoral office answerable to God, who remains the true owner of the flock. The shepherd-king image runs through Scripture and finds its fulfillment in Jesus, the Good Shepherd (John 10:11) and Son of David, who lays down his life for the sheep. Earthly rule is thus a stewardship of God's people, not personal ownership.
facets.question: What does it mean that the king is called to be a shepherd of God's people?

facets.evidence: The passage states 'David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD,' and the tradition firmly reads Davidic covenant-kingship as the foundation for the everlasting covenant of 2 Samuel 7/Psalm 89; the relational and divine-witness dimensions are the plain sense of 'before the LORD.'
facets.text: David "made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD," so that his kingship rests on a bond sworn in God's presence rather than on conquest or dynastic force. This covenantal foundation binds king and people to mutual obligation under God and anticipates the everlasting covenant God will make with David's house. Kingship in Israel is always relational and answerable to the divine witness of the covenant.
facets.question: Why is David's kingship established through a covenant before the LORD?

facets.evidence: They anointed David king over Israel, according to the LORD's word by Samuel.
facets.text: The people anoint David "according to the LORD's word by Samuel," so the human act of coronation fulfills the earlier prophetic choice made when Samuel first anointed David in Bethlehem. The community's decision does not create the king but recognizes and confirms God's prior election. God's providential word runs ahead of history and is vindicated in its own time.
facets.question: How does David's coronation fulfill God's earlier word through Samuel?

facets.evidence: The Chronicler's exilic context and the messianic-ingathering reading (including the extension to Christ the King and all nations) are inferences drawn from the text's emphasis on 'all Israel' but require historical-critical and typological arguments not present in the passage itself.
facets.text: The unity of "all Israel" gathering to one anointed king at Hebron portrays the ideal of God's scattered people made one under a single divinely-chosen head. This gathering foreshadows the messianic hope of a reunited Israel and, for the Church, the ingathering of all nations under Christ the King. The Chronicler, writing after exile, holds up this moment of national unity as a pattern of what God intends to restore.
facets.question: What is the significance of all Israel uniting under one anointed king?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: This passage recounts the anointing of David as king over all Israel at Hebron through covenant, prophetic fulfillment, and acclamation, encompassing themes of Davidic kingship, shepherd-king typology, covenantal authority, and messianic prefiguration.

[typological/scriptural | inferential]: The tribes' declaration "we are your bone and your flesh" invokes the language of Genesis 2:23, binding ruler and people in natural kinship rather than imposed dominion. This solidarity prefigures the incarnation of Christ, the Son of David, who assumed human nature so that believers could become members of his body.

[moral/scriptural | settled]: David's credibility as Israel's rightful ruler derived from a proven record of leading the nation in battle and governance before any formal coronation was granted. Legitimate authority in the Old Testament is demonstrated through faithful prior service, not merely conferred by title; his anointing confirms what his life had already warranted.

[typological/doctrinal | inferential]: God's designation of David as "shepherd of my people Israel" frames royal office as a pastoral stewardship accountable to the divine owner of the flock. This image reaches its fulfillment in Jesus the Good Shepherd (John 10:11), the greater Son of David, who lays down his life for the sheep, revealing that earthly rule is always a delegated care of God's own people.

[doctrinal/scriptural | settled]: The covenant solemnized before the LORD at Hebron grounds Davidic kingship in a sworn, witnessed bond rather than in military conquest or dynastic succession alone. This covenantal structure places king and people under mutual obligation to God and anticipates the eternal covenant God will establish with David's house, making Israelite monarchy inherently relational and divinely accountable.

[scriptural/doctrinal | explicit]: The anointing performed by the elders executes a divine commission already issued through Samuel's earlier prophetic choice of David in Bethlehem, so the community's coronation act ratifies rather than originates royal election. God's providential word precedes and governs historical events, and the people's recognition completes what divine election had already determined.

[typological/historical | inferential]: The assembly of "all Israel" beneath a single anointed head at Hebron embodies the theological ideal of God's people unified under one divinely chosen ruler. The Chronicler, addressing a post-exilic audience, presents this moment as a pattern of restoration, foreshadowing the messianic ingathering of a renewed Israel and, for the Church, the eschatological unity of all nations under Christ the King.
